entries.clue: Change plug recently (6)

blocks.note: a plug for a product on a radio show is a free ad
just arrived means arrived a moment ago

annotation.surface: Somebody has changed a plug lately.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plug' looks like the thing on the end of a kettle flex and means a piece of free publicity — what a guest does for a book on a chat show.
annotation.definitionFit: Change → ADJUST: a plain verb synonym, though a narrower one, since adjusting is changing something by a small amount rather than replacing it.

entries.clue: Unconventional knot of a tie to tell apart (13)

indicatorNotes.knot: A knot is a length of rope pulled out of its straight order into a tangle, so the letters it is applied to come out in a different order.

blocks.note: somebody unconventional does things differently from everyone else
four letters, the article included, reset in a new order

annotation.surface: An oddly knotted tie is what tells two people apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unconventional' opens the clue where fodder usually sits and is a nine-letter synonym handed over whole; only four letters are shuffled. 'Knot' reads as a noun in the picture and is the word doing the shuffling.
annotation.definitionFit: tell apart → DIFFERENTIATE: the formal verb for marking the difference between two things, which is what telling them apart amounts to.

entries.clue: Free ale, shun rum! (7)

indicatorNotes.rum: Rum is an old British adjective meaning odd or peculiar — a rum do, a rum lot — and letters called odd are not left in the order they were given.

blocks.note: seven letters, spread across two words and a comma, to be reordered

annotation.surface: A bar is giving ale away and warning drinkers off the rum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like a third drink lined up beside the ale and is the instruction; the exclamation mark keeps the sentence sounding like a bar notice. The adjective survives mainly in the phrase 'a rum do', meaning a strange business.
annotation.definitionFit: Free → UNLEASH: the verb sense of free, letting something off its leash and loose, rather than the sense of costing nothing.

entries.clue: What rounds off digit, one processed in the end (7)

indicatorNotes.processed: Something processed has been put through a machine and comes out altered, which is what happens to the order of these letters.
indicatorNotes.in: In says one piece is written inside another rather than set down beside it.

blocks.note: the tail of anything is its end, and this word opens up after its first letter
three letters put into another order before they go inside

annotation.surface: A rounding-off question, with one last item put through the works at the end of the day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Digit' is a finger or a toe as readily as a number, and the surface pushes the number. The definition then describes rather than names: what caps the end of a toe is a hard plate, not a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: The digit is a toe and the nail is the hard plate capping its end, so the definition describes the thing rather than offering a synonym.

entries.clue: Not yet constructed, wretched man due (6)

indicatorNotes.wretched: A wretched thing is in a sorry state, and letters in a sorry state are no longer standing in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: six letters across two words, all of them wanted

annotation.surface: A miserable man is due to turn up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wretched' is perfectly at home describing the man and is the word doing the shuffling; the comma is the only mark showing where the definition stops. An unmade road is one that was never surfaced, which is the sense of 'not yet constructed' at work here.
annotation.definitionFit: Not yet constructed → UNMADE: the plain negative of made, used of a road never surfaced and of anything that has yet to be put together.

entries.clue: Say total (5)

blocks.note: the verb for producing words aloud
complete, absolute, the intensifier that goes in front of nonsense or chaos

annotation.surface: A request to read the total out loud.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words and two definitions, with no machinery between them — both halves have to be tested as senses of one word. 'Say' is a warning sign here: it usually asks for a sound-alike, and this time it is a straight synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Say → UTTER as a verb, to speak something aloud; total → UTTER as an adjective meaning complete, as in utter nonsense.

entries.clue: Doctor has baby to clear away (3,2)

blocks.note: the MO is the Medical Officer, the doctor attached to a British army unit or a ship
a dog's baby is a pup

annotation.surface: A doctor is handed a baby to see to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is an anagram indicator far more often than it is a piece of the answer, and nothing in this clue is shuffled. 'Baby' wants a human infant and turns out to be a young dog.
annotation.definitionFit: clear away → MOP UP: to mop up is to clear away what is left behind, whether that is spilt liquid or the last of a job.

entries.clue: Supervise present-day power supply (6,7)

blocks.note: to direct an operation is to supervise it
current affairs are present-day ones

annotation.surface: Someone is to oversee the electricity network of today.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary words doing ordinary jobs, so the work is seeing that 'present-day' is a synonym rather than scene-setting. DC is what a battery delivers, as against the alternating current that comes out of a wall socket.
annotation.definitionFit: power supply → DIRECT CURRENT: electricity flowing steadily one way, the form a battery or a solar cell supplies, named by what it does rather than by a synonym.

entries.clue: At first loud, articulate and rich (8)

indicatorNotes.first: First asks for the opening letter of the word beside it and nothing more, so only one letter of 'At' comes through.

blocks.note: the word gives up only the letter it starts with
f is forte on a score, the musician's mark for playing loudly
somebody articulate is fluent in speech

annotation.surface: A man who starts out loud, speaks well and has money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At first' reads as 'to begin with' and is really an instruction to take a single letter. The musical marks are worth owning for good: f is loud, p is soft, and ff is louder still.
annotation.definitionFit: rich → AFFLUENT: the polite adjective for having plenty of money, applied to people and to the neighbourhoods they live in.

entries.clue: Soft old vessel at sports ground (4)

blocks.note: p is piano on a score, the musician's mark for playing softly
the vessel Noah built, and the oldest boat in the language

annotation.surface: An old boat is sitting at a sports ground.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Soft' and 'loud' both come off a musical score, p and f, and both turn up constantly. British football clubs name their grounds with this word — Newcastle play at St James' Park, Nottingham Forest at the City Ground.
annotation.definitionFit: sports ground → PARK: open ground kept for games, and the word British clubs put on their grounds, as in St James' Park.

entries.clue: Huge as a flipping jewel (4)

indicatorNotes.flipping: To flip a thing is to turn it over end for end, so the letters it applies to are read the other way round.

blocks.note: the article counts as a letter of the material, not as joinery
a gem is a jewel

annotation.surface: Something is as big as a blooming great jewel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' does two jobs: it is the mild British swear word the sentence wants and the turn-around the wordplay needs. The little 'a' goes into the reversal too — leave it out and the count comes up short.
annotation.definitionFit: Huge → MEGA: the informal adjective for enormous, taken from the scientific prefix meaning a million.

entries.clue: A price as ridiculous in area that's high (8)

indicatorNotes.ridiculous: What is ridiculous is out of all proper proportion, and letters out of proportion are letters out of their proper places.

blocks.note: eight letters counting the opening article, all of them wanted

annotation.surface: A laughable asking price somewhere high up.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue opens with its own material, which is why the capital A reads as an article and is really a letter. A country's airspace is the sky above it that it claims and polices, so 'area' is doing duty for a volume of air.
annotation.definitionFit: area that's high → AIRSPACE: the stretch of sky above a country or an airport, an area reckoned in the air rather than on the ground.

entries.clue: Deadly section of toilet halved (6)

indicatorNotes.section of: A section of something is a piece cut out of it in one unbroken run, so the letters wanted sit consecutively in the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run starts inside the first word and carries straight on over the space

annotation.surface: A deadly piece of a toilet that has been cut in two.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Halved' looks like an instruction to take half a word and is only there to lengthen the hiding place, contributing its first three letters and nothing else. The gap between the two words is the cover: the eye stops at a space.
annotation.definitionFit: Deadly → LETHAL: plain synonyms, both adjectives saying a dose or a blow is enough to kill — a lethal dose, a deadly dose.

entries.clue: One moment without energy, using credit (2,4)

indicatorNotes.without: To be without a thing is to be lacking it, so the word in front gives up the letter named next.

blocks.note: ONE spelled out as printed, then stripped of the letter named next
E is the physicist's symbol for energy, and it is the letter that drops out
back in a tick means back in a moment

annotation.surface: A moment's pause from somebody with no energy left.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the deletion and 'One' is the word it empties, and neither looks like machinery in a sentence about being tired. On tick is British shop slang for buying now and paying later, from the tick a shopkeeper put against your name in his book.
annotation.definitionFit: using credit → ON TICK: the British idiom for taking goods now and settling the bill afterwards, the shopkeeper's running tally being the tick.

entries.clue: Sweeping cocaine away (7)

indicatorNotes.away: Letters sent away are letters that do not stay where they were put, and these land in fresh positions.

blocks.note: seven letters, exactly the number wanted, to be put in another order

annotation.surface: Somebody is sweeping a spill of cocaine away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sweeping away' reads as one phrase and the clue splits it down the middle: the first word is the definition and the last is the instruction. The adjective means on the scale of an ocean, which is how it reaches 'sweeping'.
annotation.definitionFit: Sweeping → OCEANIC: a change or a view called oceanic is one on the scale of an ocean, vast and all-embracing, which is the sense 'sweeping' carries in sweeping reforms.

entries.clue: Neat addition to considerable amount (4,3)

blocks.note: a neat room is a tidy one
the sum is what an addition comes to

annotation.surface: A neat little addition on top of an already large amount.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Neat' and 'addition' both sound like arithmetic and neither is: the answer is money. In British use a tidy amount means a sizeable one, which is why the definition says considerable.
annotation.definitionFit: considerable amount → TIDY SUM: a British idiom for a good deal of money, 'tidy' carrying its informal sense of sizeable rather than neat.

entries.clue: Sit astride, right back in the seat (8)

indicatorNotes.back: Taken as an instruction rather than as part of a footballer's position, back sends the letters in front of it the other way round.
indicatorNotes.in: In says the piece just built is written inside the next one instead of beside it.

blocks.note: the seat on a horse or a bicycle, which opens up after its first letter
Rt is the standard short form of right, as in the Rt Hon before a senior MP's name

annotation.surface: Somebody sitting astride, pushed right back in the seat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right back' is a defender's position in British football, which is the trap; here it is an abbreviation with a turn-around instruction after it. Rt is how Parliament writes the word, in the Rt Hon that precedes a privy counsellor's name.
annotation.definitionFit: Sit astride → STRADDLE: to straddle a horse, a fence or a ditch is to sit or stand with one leg on either side of it.

entries.clue: Some shank, leg or joint (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a thing is a part of it taken as it stands, so what is wanted sits unbroken inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run begins inside the first word and carries on over the comma

annotation.surface: A butcher's list of cuts — shank, leg or joint.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a butcher's counter, where a joint is a piece of meat for roasting rather than a hinge in the body. The comma sitting inside the hiding place is the best cover a setter has, because the eye stops at punctuation.
annotation.definitionFit: joint → ANKLE: a joint is where two bones meet and move against each other, and the ankle is the hinge between leg and foot.

entries.clue: Society girl has a right to refuse entry (5)

blocks.note: a deb is a debutante, a young woman formally presented to high society
the article taken straight into the letters
r = right, the one-letter short form used on maps and in instructions

annotation.surface: A debutante is entitled to turn people away at the door.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a sentence about privilege — she has a right — while the clue is three pieces stacked, with 'a' counting as a letter rather than joinery. The London deb season, with its presentations at court, ended in 1958, but the word kept its place in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: To debar someone is to shut them out of a place or an activity — the formal verb for what a doorman does.

entries.clue: 500 put on Noah's boat, at night? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is an adjective and the definition an adverbial phrase, so the two cannot be swapped in a sentence; the question mark is the setter conceding that night is when the thing holds rather than a word for it.

blocks.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals
the boat built for the flood in Genesis

annotation.surface: Five hundred animals are loaded onto the ark by night.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is a when and not a what. Roman numerals repay memorising: D is 500, C a hundred, M a thousand, and setters reach for them whenever a clue names a round number.
annotation.definitionFit: Night is the stretch of day without sunlight, so 'at night' points at the condition rather than naming it, as the question mark concedes.

entries.clue: Boy making impression (4)

blocks.note: an ordinary man's first name, shared with one of the four gospel writers
the trace a pressed or scraped thing leaves on a surface

annotation.surface: A boy who leaves an impression on people.
annotation.walkthrough: Two definitions with one word joining them, and the joke is that the joined sentence is true of the answer. 'Boy' could be any name in the book, so it is the second half that pins the four letters down.
annotation.definitionFit: Boy → MARK is an ordinary man's first name; impression → MARK is the dent or smudge something pressed leaves behind.

entries.clue: Brian set off with handrail (8)

indicatorNotes.off: Something off is not as it should be — milk goes off — and letters that are off are not standing in their proper order.

blocks.note: eight letters, a name and a verb, to be reordered

annotation.surface: Brian sets off holding on to the handrail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as one phrase — Brian leaving the house — and the clue splits it: 'set' is material and 'off' is the instruction. The word names the rail itself, after the balusters, the little uprights holding it up.
annotation.definitionFit: handrail → BANISTER: the rail you run your hand along at the side of a staircase, which is the handrail a house actually has.

entries.clue: Remote sort of rock from outer space (6)

indicatorNotes.sort of: To sort things is to put them into a new order, so 'sort of' asks for the word in front of it rearranged.

blocks.note: six letters, exactly the number wanted, taken as printed

annotation.surface: Some remote kind of rock, far out in space.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' reads as a hedge — a remote sort of rock — and is the instruction, which is where setters like to hide a shuffle. Strictly the word names the streak of light: the lump is a meteoroid in flight and a meteorite once it has landed.
annotation.definitionFit: rock from outer space → METEOR: in general use the word for a lump of space rock streaking through our sky, the shooting star anyone would point at.

entries.clue: Body with tail, ring to wake up (4,2)

blocks.note: the heavenly body that trails a tail of dust and gas behind it
O is the round letter that stands in for a ring

annotation.surface: Somebody gives the tailed creature a ring to wake it up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring' wants to be the telephone call the surface promises and is the shape of a letter instead. The answer is what a person does after fainting, which is why the definition is a phrasal verb rather than a single word.
annotation.definitionFit: wake up → COME TO: to come to is to regain consciousness after fainting or a blow, the waking that follows being knocked out.
